sample_size.excerpt: Baseline characteristics for the 450,207 participants and 418,060 included in the main analysis were similar (Supplementary Table S3).

cases.excerpt: For gender-specific cancers, we identified 9,111 (4.8%) prostate cancers and 475 (3%) other site-specific cancers in males; 447 (0.2%) cervical cancers, 9,068 (4.0%) breast cancers, 843 (0.4%) ovarian cancers, 1,294 (0.6%) endometrium cancers, and 322 (0.1%) other site-specific cancers in females.
cases.location: Results, Glucosamine use and risk of cancer paragraph

effect_size.excerpt: In the full-adjusted model, glucosamine use was statistically significantly associated with increased risk for overall cancer (HR, 1.04; 95% CI, 1.01–1.06), prostate cancer (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01–1.13), and skin cancer (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07–1.15), but with reduced risk for lung cancer (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79–0.97).

disease_scope_review.endpoint_excerpt: During a median of 12.5 years follow-up, glucosamine use was significantly associated with an increased risk of overall cancer [HR, 1.04; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.01-1.06], skin cancer (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.07-1.15), and prostate cancer (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.13), and with a reduced risk of lung cancer (HR, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79-0.97) after adjusting for potential confounders.
disease_scope_review.reason: The HR of 1.07 is explicitly reported for incident prostate cancer generally, without an aggressive subtype definition. This row duplicates the same association represented by the other supplied row rather than a separate population.

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.06 (95% CI: 1.01–1.11), suggesting that glucosamine is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer. These findings were supported by low between-study heterogeneity (I² = 0.00%), indicating consistent findings across the included studies.
